hints.title: Company Max Salary Partition
hints.text: Compute max(salary) over (partition by company_id) to establish the tax tier for each company.

hints.title: Tiered Tax Calculation
hints.text: If max salary < 1000 tax is 0%; if between 1000 and 10000 tax is 24%; if > 10000 tax is 49%.

hints.title: Rounding Net Salary
hints.text: Compute round(salary * (1 - tax_rate)) as the post-tax salary for each employee.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH CompanyMax AS (
    SELECT company_id, employee_id, employee_name, salary,
           MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY company_id) AS max_sal
    FROM Salaries
)
SELECT company_id, employee_id, employee_name,
       ROUND(salary * (1 - CASE
           WHEN max_sal < 1000 THEN 0.00
           WHEN max_sal <= 10000 THEN 0.24
           ELSE 0.49
       END)) AS salary
FROM CompanyMax;
```

variables: N: number of employee records in Salaries
complexity.notes: Window aggregation partitions employees by company_id in linear time followed by scalar math.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Correlated subqueries to find company max salary repeat table scans for every individual employee.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Window MAX computes company ceilings without reducing row cardinality.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Window function MAX() OVER (PARTITION BY company_id) combined with CASE tax arithmetic.

solutions.approach: PostgreSQL Window Function Salary Tax Adjustment

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def calculate_salaries(salaries: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    salaries['max_sal'] = salaries.groupby('company_id')['salary'].transform('max')
    def get_tax(max_s):
        if max_s < 1000: return 0.0
        if max_s <= 10000: return 0.24
        return 0.49
    salaries['tax'] = salaries['max_sal'].apply(get_tax)
    salaries['salary'] = (salaries['salary'] * (1 - salaries['tax'])).round()
    return salaries[['company_id', 'employee_id', 'employee_name', 'salary']]
